title: Best Phishing & Social Engineering Tools Compared
metaDescription: Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and KnowBe4 compared on email scanning, link and attachment protection and phishing training.
intro: Phishing emails are harder to spot than they used to be, with AI-written messages and convincing brand impersonation. This page compares four business email-security and awareness-training tools on the same six criteria, and each rating is worked out from the table.

products.name: Proofpoint Email Protection
products.tagline: Email security for large organizations, with link and attachment sandboxing
cons: Phishing simulation and awareness training are a separate product (Proofpoint ZenGuide)

products.name: Microsoft Defender for Office 365
products.tagline: Email and collaboration protection for Microsoft 365
products.pricing: Plan 1 $2/user/month; Plan 2 $5/user/month (also included in some Microsoft 365 plans)
pros: Safe Links and Safe Attachments features
Low per-user price, and included in some Microsoft 365 plans
cons: Attack simulation training and automated investigation need Plan 2

products.name: KnowBe4 Security Awareness
products.tagline: Security awareness training with simulated phishing
products.pricing: Annual per-user subscription in four tiers (Silver to Diamond); quote-based
cons: Focuses on training rather than prevention
Can be overwhelming for small teams

products.name: Mimecast Email Security
products.tagline: Cloud-based email security with threat intelligence
pros: Email continuity and archiving available on the same platform
cons: Can be expensive for smaller organizations
Awareness training and phishing simulation are an add-on (Mimecast Engage)

verdict.summary: On these six criteria Proofpoint Email Protection scores highest, with Mimecast Email Security close behind: both scan email, links and attachments in real time and draw on large threat-intelligence networks, and both sell phishing simulation training as a separate product. Microsoft Defender for Office 365 comes next, rated good rather than excellent on each criterion; it is the natural choice if you already use Microsoft 365, and Plan 2 includes attack simulation training. KnowBe4 scores lowest here because it trains people rather than filtering email, but it has the best phishing simulation score of the four, so it pairs well with an email-security product.

bestFor.reason: Highest score here: advanced threat detection, URL and attachment sandboxing, and detailed threat reporting

Built for Microsoft 365 at a per-user price; Plan 2 adds attack simulation training

bestFor.reason: Large phishing simulation library, training modules and detailed training analytics

pro_tips: Always verify sender identity by calling the organization directly using a number from their official website, not from the email.
Look for subtle spelling mistakes in URLs - attackers often use domains like 'arnazon.com' instead of 'amazon.com' to fool users.
Enable two-factor authentication on all important accounts to add an extra security layer even if passwords are compromised.
Use a password manager: it fills your password only on the real site, so a look-alike login page gets nothing.
Be especially cautious of urgent requests for money, passwords, or personal information - legitimate companies rarely create artificial urgency.

faqs.question: What's the difference between phishing and spear phishing?
faqs.answer: Regular phishing uses generic messages sent to many people, while spear phishing targets specific individuals with personalized information to appear more legitimate. Spear phishing attacks are typically more dangerous because they're harder to detect.

faqs.question: Can antivirus software protect against phishing attacks?
faqs.answer: Partly. Many security suites now include web protection that blocks known phishing sites, and mainstream browsers warn you about known phishing pages too (Google Safe Browsing in Chrome, Firefox and Safari; Microsoft Defender SmartScreen in Edge). Email security tools like the ones on this page stop many phishing emails before they arrive. None of them catches everything, so a password manager that fills passwords only on the real site and two-factor authentication are worth having as well.

faqs.question: How can I tell if a suspicious email is actually a phishing attempt?
faqs.answer: Check for urgency tactics, generic greetings, suspicious links or attachments, requests for personal information, and sender address mismatches. When in doubt, contact the organization directly through official channels to verify.

faqs.question: Are mobile devices more vulnerable to phishing attacks?
faqs.answer: Yes, mobile devices can be more vulnerable because URLs are harder to examine on small screens, and users are more likely to click quickly without careful inspection. Use browsers with phishing protection and be extra cautious on mobile.

faqs.question: What should I do if I accidentally clicked a phishing link?
faqs.answer: Immediately disconnect from the internet, run a security scan, change passwords for any accounts that might be compromised, monitor your accounts for suspicious activity, and report the incident to your IT department or the targeted organization.
